About this citation

Epictetus wrote nothing. The Discourses were transcribed and edited by his pupil Arrian, who states that he recorded what he heard and left the reasoning as it stood; the Handbook is Arrian's own selection. Attribution to Epictetus is therefore via Arrian in every case.

#### About Epictetus

Epictetus (c. 50–c.

### Interpretation

Enchiridion 17 applies the distinction the handbook opens with, between what is up to us and what is not. The part — poor or rich, lame or in office, long or short — is assigned; performing it well is ours. Epictetus, born a slave, is not recommending passivity about one's circumstances but relocating dignity: it lies in how a role is played, which no one can take away, rather than in which role one was given, which anyone might.

#### Why it matters

It is a useful check on resentment at work or in a family: separate the part you did not choose from the performance you do. The first may be worth changing; the second is already entirely yours, and it is usually where the real difference is made.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Remember that you are an actor in a…”?

“Remember that you are an actor in a…” comes from Discourses and Enchiridion, 17 (c. 108 CE (recorded by Arrian)), attributed to Epictetus.

#### What does Epictetus mean by fate?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Epictetus and Seneca), fate is framed through Stoicism and Philosophy of Will. Some passages define fate; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through fate.
